newsitem.title: UK: Mark crosses struggle near low, Buba shows concern.
newsitem.headline: Mark crosses struggle near low, Buba shows concern.

text.p: The mark was trapped near s session lows on most crosses in European afternoon trade, gaining little strength from a top-level Bundesbank official's comments expressing concerns about the mark.
The mark crosses were generally tracking the German currency's slide against the dollar, traders said.

The mark slid to its lowest level against the dollar in nearly eight years earlier. Although the mark regained a tiny bit of ground against the dollar on the comments made by Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing, it slid back soon after and the mark crosses followed suit.

Issing said in an interview with "Boerse-Online" magazine that the mark's exchange rate was one of the most important indicators for the Bundesbank, and that the central bank's main priority was the mark's stability.
He also said rapid movements in currencies rather than particular levels were of concern to the Bundesbank.

"Dollar/mark slipped a touch on Issing's comments at first, but it came back up when he said there was no particular level (that was of concern to the Buba)...And the mark crosses seem to be taking the strain," said Pat Magill, head of corporate trading at Daiwa Europe.

This provided no respite for the mark crosses, and mark/lira was trading near its session low of 978.25/55 at 1310 GMT against its late Monday European level of 979.80. Mark/Swiss franc was at 81.58/61 centimes against 81.70.

Mark/French franc bucked the trend, however, as the dollar's rally against the franc to its highest in nearly eight years towed mark/Paris higher with it. Mark/Paris was just off its session high at 3.3773/78 against Monday's 3.3733.

Issing also referred to the Bundesbank's policy on money market tenders, which had been the focus for market speculation in recent days. He said the central bank could not steer policy to match money market expectations, and that there was no direct link between dollar rates and monetary policy.
Earlier today, the Bundesbank flouted market expectations by making no reference to future securities repurchase tenders when it conducted today's fixed-rate weekly repo tender.
The market had been speculating the central bank could offer a variable rate repo today as well as the fixed-rate one, or set the terms for next week's tender to offer a variable repo.

Wariness that the authorities could take such steps to allow German market rates to rise had bolstered the mark on the crosses earlier. But it shed these gains rapidly when the Bundesbank made no immediate comment on money market activities.

"For now, people are selling off the marks they bought up on the speculation over today's repo tender and adjusting positions for the very short term regardless (of what might happen at the next tender)," said Junpei Yamamoto, head of forex at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
The market was now looking to the next tender on August 12, with the mark's movements over the next week seen key.
A parallel repo -- conducting tenders at both variable and fixed rates -- is seen as a likely scenario, if not at the next tender then sometime in the near future.

"In the process of convergence for EMU...it looks like it might be difficult to make short-term rates converge at a lower level. So it's quite likely they will make this happen by letting German rates rise closer to those of other countries through a variable repo," BOT-Mitsubishi's Yamamoto said.
